newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish ruling coalition rocked over tax, abortion.
newsitem.headline: Polish ruling coalition rocked over tax, abortion.

text.p: Poland's ex-communist Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz furiously accused his party's coalition partners on Thursday of betraying a vital deal on taxes and harming the nation's finances.

The sudden clash between the premier's Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) and the smaller Polish Peasant party exposed the ever-deepening rifts in the coalition which has ruled Poland since 1993 elections, but repeatedly come close to collapse.

The Peasants backed an unexpected motion by a small socialist party to lower the bottom rate of personal income tax, throwing the government's carefully-laid financial plans into disarray just as it was near to clinching the 1997 budget.

"This vote is a disgrace to the majority in parliament," Cimoszewicz told the chamber after deputies approved a bill changing taxes, depending on income, to 17, 20, 33 and 45 percent from the current 21, 33 and 45 percent.

"Here in this chamber there have been many debates, we quarrelled...but one rule was respected: where the state's economic interest is at stake, where responsibility for the state's financial structure is at stake, there is no room for political games," Cimoszewicz told parliamentarians.

The confusion in parliament -- where the Peasants helped smaller parties to defeat the SLD, which has the largest bloc vote -- followed just after most of the Peasants also voted against an SLD-backed bill easing abortion.
But the leaders of the SLD and Peasants, Jozef Oleksy and Waldemar Pawlak, told reporters after the vote that the coalition was not about to fall apart.
The controversial abortion bill passed by a small majority.

The Peasants' stance on abortion has however left open the possibility they could form an alternative coalition with rightist, pro-Catholic Church parties grouped around the Solidarity trade union, after elections due in September 1997.
The Peasants have already formed a non-aggression pact with the Solidarity alliance, which opposed the abortion bill, and which is running about level with the SLD in opinion polls.
Cimoszewicz said the support for the 17-percent level was an electioneering gesture by the Peasants and other parties, and could not be sustained by current budget planning.

He said the Peasants had reneged on a behind-the-scenes deal over the tax bill, clinched on Wednesday, under which they had agreed to back the government tax plans in exchange for support for a bill subsidising fuel for farmers.
The new 17 percent tax level, which will help many voters on low incomes, can still be blocked by the Senate or by President Aleksander Kwasniewski -- a former SLD leader.
But if upheld, it could cost the 1997 budget 4.5 billion zlotys ($1.60 billion) in lost revenues, Finance Minister Grzegorz Kolodko told deputies before the vote.

He said the new tax level and the resulting revenue gap would hamper work on the budget, to be submitted to parliament next week, because it would either mean a sharp cut in spending or a rise in the budget deficit which would boost inflation.
